strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and presents a coherent coarse-to-fine registration pipeline: feature-space filtering provides global robustness, while anchor-guided geometric proxies and robust nearest-neighbor refinement improve local alignment.

The reported accuracy-efficiency tradeoff is strong. Across 3DMatch, 3DLoMatch, and KITTI with both FPFH and FCGF, DualReg is consistently among the best in registration recall and reports the lowest RMSE, rotation error, and translation error in most settings, while being substantially faster than MAC-family methods.

The evaluation includes indoor, low-overlap indoor, and outdoor benchmarks, two descriptor types, numerous recent baselines, CPU runtime measurements, qualitative examples, and component ablations. Tables IV and V provide useful evidence that filtering, refinement, anchors, and geometric correspondences each contribute.

The method is training-free and built from relatively standard operations such as distance tests, SVD, nearest-neighbor search, and iteratively reweighted estimation, which could make it practically useful and easier to deploy than learned registration pipelines.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate rather than compelling. The pipeline largely combines one-point consensus filtering related to TCF, probability-guided three-point sampling derived from BANSAC, and an anchor-restricted robust ICP procedure. The manuscript describes this combination as a novel dual-space paradigm but does not sharply establish what conceptual capability is unavailable from a TCF/BANSAC initialization followed by robust local ICP.

Several algorithmic details are insufficient or internally inconsistent, materially limiting reproducibility. Algorithm 1 updates s_ci^(k+1) from s_ci^(k-1), does not specify score propagation for correspondences outside the accepted set, and leaves the construction cost/procedure for the all-pairs condition in Eq. (5) unclear. The refinement delegates probability updates and sampling details to BANSAC, while Eq. (10) uses an undefined or ambiguous |C| rather than clearly specifying the active correspondence set.

The symmetry test lacks justification. Rejecting an entire consensus set whenever unconstrained orthogonal Procrustes yields determinant -1 is only a heuristic: noise, outliers, rank deficiency, or nearly planar geometry can also change the determinant. No analysis or targeted experiment demonstrates that this test reliably detects symmetry rather than discarding valid hypotheses.

The robust optimization has unresolved edge cases and ambiguities. The proxy sets are introduced as sets of neighborhoods but later treated as a single point set without explaining duplicates or correspondence scope; sigma can become zero or unstable when the selected residuals are very small; and the stopping expression takes a square root of a transformation-matrix norm while mixing rotation and translation units. No convergence or numerical-stability discussion is provided.

The experimental protocol does not quantify randomness or tuning sensitivity. RANSAC-based results are reported without seeds, repeated trials, variances, or confidence intervals, and important parameters vary substantially by dataset and descriptor, such as alpha=0.2 versus 0.9/0.95 and lambda=0.05 versus 1.0, without a validation protocol or sensitivity analysis. Small recall differences, including 98.20% versus 98.02%, therefore cannot be interpreted confidently.

Runtime evidence is incomplete: it is not explicit whether feature extraction, normal estimation, downsampling, and proxy construction are all included, and there is no scaling analysis with correspondence or point-cloud size. The claimed likely speed advantage over TurboReg is inferred by combining runtime ratios from different implementations rather than measured directly and should not support a comparative conclusion.

The definitions and aggregation of RMSE, rotation error, and translation error are underspecified, particularly whether errors are averaged over all pairs or only successful registrations. If computed only on successful pairs, comparing the error columns between methods with substantially different recall can be misleading. These reporting issues weaken the otherwise promising empirical case.

The prose repeatedly overstates the evidence with claims such as perfect synergy, unprecedented precision, and a new benchmark. This is primarily a presentation issue, but the lack of code or a stated release plan, exact baseline configuration details, and complete pseudocode also makes independent reproduction difficult. Overall, the strong reported results place the work near the acceptance boundary, but the methodological underspecification, unvalidated heuristics, and uncertain statistical and runtime protocol prevent a weak-accept recommendation in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem and presents a coherent coarse-to-fine pipeline combining global feature correspondences with local geometric refinement.

The empirical results are promising across two indoor benchmarks and KITTI, using both handcrafted FPFH and learned FCGF features. In particular, the method substantially improves over the very fast TCF baseline while remaining much faster than MAC-family methods; the reported 3.91 s versus 0.12 s KITTI-FPFH runtime supports the advertised 32× speedup over MAC.

Evaluation includes registration recall, several accuracy measures, CPU runtime, qualitative examples, and component ablations. Testing low-overlap 3DLoMatch and two descriptor types is useful evidence that the method is not tied to one easy setting.
The approach requires no additional learned model and could therefore be practically useful when a lightweight CPU registration backend is needed.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The main ingredients are pairwise distance/normal compatibility, a one-correspondence consensus procedure related to TCF, BANSAC-style three-point sampling, neighborhood extraction around anchors, and robust ICP-like alternating optimization. The paper does not clearly establish a substantial conceptual advance beyond this assembly of existing ideas.

The proposed “symmetry check” is not technically justified. A determinant of −1 for the unconstrained orthogonal Procrustes solution only indicates that the best fitted orthogonal map is improper; it does not demonstrate that the two sets are mirror-symmetric. For rank-deficient or nearly planar configurations—common in indoor point clouds—the SVD null-space signs can also make this test unstable. Discarding the entire consensus set on this basis can therefore reject valid rigid correspondences, yet no degeneracy analysis or controlled experiment is provided.

The efficiency argument is incomplete. Reducing the number of possible samples from O(n^3) to O(n) does not establish the algorithm's total complexity: constructing Eq. (5) appears to require checking every candidate against every member of the initial consensus set, potentially O(n^2) per sampled correspondence. Neither a complexity analysis nor scaling experiments over the number of correspondences are reported.

Several algorithmic details are inconsistent or underspecified. Algorithm 1 updates s^(k+1) from s^(k−1), Eq. (10) uses an ambiguous |C| rather than |C_I|, and the BANSAC probability update is delegated to another paper despite those probabilities later determining the top-40% subset used to set sigma. The statement that residuals beyond 3 sigma are “ignored” is also inaccurate for the Gaussian weight, which remains nonzero. These issues materially impair reproducibility.

The experimental gains are overstated and lack uncertainty estimates despite randomized sampling. On 3DMatch-FPFH, recall merely ties TurboReg at 84.10%; on 3DMatch-FCGF, MAC has higher recall; and the claimed best KITTI-FPFH recall exceeds MAC++ by only 0.18 percentage points—approximately one case among 555 pairs. Results from repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are absent.

The ablations do not consistently support the claim that every component is beneficial. On 3DLoMatch-FCGF, removing refinement gives higher recall than the full model (60.8% versus 60.5%); removing anchors gives slightly lower RMSE (7.74 versus 7.76 cm); and patch-wise processing gives higher FPFH recall (41.9% versus 41.6%). There is also no sensitivity study for strongly dataset- and descriptor-dependent parameters such as alpha, which changes from 0.2 to 0.95.

Runtime reproducibility is insufficient. The manuscript does not specify whether feature extraction, normal estimation, downsampling, proxy construction, and correspondence generation are included, nor does it provide random seeds, thread settings per method, full baseline configurations, or released code. The inferred speed advantage over TurboReg is based on ratios from different measurements and is not direct evidence.

The evaluation covers standard datasets but lacks controlled stress tests for the specific robustness claims, such as varying inlier ratio, noise, overlap, normal corruption, correspondence count, and planar degeneracy. The method itself acknowledges dependence on the initial descriptors, yet the point at which filtering fails is not characterized.

The exposition contains excessive promotional language such as “perfect synergy,” “unprecedented precision,” and “overwhelming advantages.” More precise reporting of tradeoffs and failure cases would improve clarity, although this presentation issue is secondary to the technical and evidential concerns above.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and presents a coherent pipeline: inexpensive feature-space filtering supplies anchors, while local geometric proxies and robust dual-space optimization improve final alignment.

Results are consistently strong across 3DMatch, the low-overlap 3DLoMatch, and KITTI, using both handcrafted FPFH and learned FCGF correspondences. The method attains the best reported error metrics in all six dataset-feature settings while remaining substantially faster than accuracy-oriented methods such as MAC and MAC++.
The accuracy-efficiency tradeoff is compelling. Examples include 93.59% recall at 0.46 s on 3DMatch-FCGF, 60.47% at 0.16 s on 3DLoMatch-FCGF, and 98.20% at 0.12 s on KITTI-FPFH.

The component studies are useful: Table IV separately examines tangential consistency, symmetry checking, and BANSAC sampling, while Table V evaluates coarse filtering, refinement, anchors, geometric correspondences, and proxy aggregation.

The method is training-free, CPU-compatible, and works with different feature extractors, which increases its practical usefulness. The manuscript also identifies reasonable limitations concerning dependence on initial feature matches and use of a fixed proxy radius.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is incomplete. The probability update and weighted sampling in the refinement stage are deferred to BANSAC rather than specified, random seeds and repeated-run variance are absent, and no code-release statement is provided. This matters because both filtering stages are stochastic.

The runtime protocol needs greater precision. It is unclear whether reported times include normal estimation, proxy construction, nearest-neighbor data structures, and other preprocessing. The comparison to TurboReg is inferred from separately reported speed ratios rather than measured directly and should not support a firm speed-ranking claim.

Several important hyperparameters are dataset-specific, especially alpha, which changes from 0.2 on 3DMatch to 0.9 or 0.95 on KITTI/3DLoMatch. No sensitivity analysis or validation protocol is given, leaving cross-dataset robustness and tuning cost uncertain.

The symmetry test is insufficiently justified. A negative determinant from unconstrained orthogonal Procrustes indicates that an improper transform fits better; under noise, outliers, or degeneracy, it does not by itself prove planar symmetry. Discarding the entire consensus set may therefore reject valid matches, and the paper provides no failure analysis.

Some technical definitions are ambiguous or inconsistent: Algorithm 1 updates s^(k+1) from s^(k-1), Eq. (10) uses an undefined correspondence set C and the current rather than clearly best consensus, and the construction of the pairwise subset in Eq. (5) is not operationally specified. The Gaussian weight is also said to ignore residuals beyond 3 sigma although it never becomes zero.

The ablations do not entirely support every narrative claim. Removing refinement slightly improves recall in several Table V settings, and the full method is not uniformly best in recall or runtime. Table IV reports only filtered-set inlier ratio, not downstream registration or filtering cost, and excludes 3DMatch.

No uncertainty estimates or repeated-trial statistics are reported. Several recall differences are only 0.1–0.6 percentage points, so claims such as setting a new benchmark are stronger than the available evidence warrants.

The approach is an effective integration of established ingredients—one-point consistency filtering, BANSAC-style sampling, robust ICP weighting, and SVD estimation—but the conceptual novelty of each individual component is moderate. The contribution is strongest as a well-performing system rather than a fundamentally new estimator.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and practically useful coarse-to-fine registration pipeline: inexpensive correspondence filtering provides anchors, local geometric proxies increase effective overlap, and robust joint optimization improves the final transformation.

The empirical evaluation is substantial, covering 3DMatch, 3DLoMatch, and KITTI with both hand-crafted FPFH and learned FCGF correspondences, alongside numerous optimization- and learning-based competitors.

The method achieves the best reported RMSE, rotation error, and translation error in all six dataset/feature configurations. Registration recall is also strong: best in two configurations and close to the best in several others, such as 60.86% versus 61.09% on 3DLoMatch with FCGF.
The CPU efficiency results are compelling. For example, on KITTI with FPFH, the method takes 0.12 s versus 3.91 s for MAC while improving recall and all reported error metrics.

Ablations separately examine fast filtering, three-point refinement, anchor and geometric terms, and patch-wise versus aggregated proxies. Runtime breakdowns, parameter sweeps, and tests with different normal-estimation settings further strengthen the evidence.
The method is clearly motivated and generally well explained, and its reliance on conventional C++/PCL/Eigen components makes a practical implementation plausible.
weaknesses: The conceptual originality is moderate. One-point RANSAC is already used by TCF, probability-weighted three-point sampling is adopted from BANSAC, and the final stage resembles robust ICP/IRLS. The main novelty is their integration with anchor-localized proxy sets rather than a fundamentally new estimator.

The central dual-space claim lacks the most informative controls: standard ICP or robust ICP initialized by the same filtered transformation, and competing global estimators followed by the same local refinement. Because only the proposed method receives its specialized refinement, the experiments do not establish how much of the accuracy advantage comes from the proposed proxy construction rather than generic post-refinement.

Several algorithmic details impede exact reproduction. Equation (5) does not state the domain of the universally quantified correspondence; Algorithm 1 updates s^(k+1) from s^(k-1), inconsistent with the main text; non-selected score updates are unspecified; and the probability update in the refinement stage is delegated to BANSAC rather than fully instantiated. Equation (15) also reuses lambda without defining its refinement-specific value.

The method uses noticeably dataset- and feature-specific settings, including alpha values of 0.2, 0.9, and 0.95 and lambda values of 0.05 indoors and 1.0 outdoors. Sensitivity analysis is conducted only on 3DMatch with FCGF, so it does not substantiate robustness around the more extreme settings used for low-overlap and outdoor cases.

The proposed algorithm is stochastic, but no seeds, repeated-run averages, or uncertainty are reported. This matters because several recall differences underlying best or near-best claims are small, such as 93.65% versus 93.72% and 60.86% versus 61.09%.

Runtime accounting is insufficiently explicit about preprocessing such as normal estimation, voxel downsampling, and proxy construction. CPU/GPU results are marked, but the claimed speed advantage over TurboReg is extrapolated from relative MAC timings rather than measured directly.

The stated failure mode at extremely low inlier ratios is important but only lightly characterized; controlled evaluation over outlier structure, overlap, noise, and normal corruption would better identify when the largest-consensus assumption breaks.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem and presents a coherent, training-free pipeline combining correspondence filtering with local geometric refinement.
The empirical coverage is reasonably broad: three established benchmarks, both handcrafted FPFH and learned FCGF correspondences, and numerous optimization- and learning-based competitors.

The reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off is promising. For example, the method obtains 98.20% recall on KITTI with FPFH in 0.12 s, versus 97.48% and 3.91 s for MAC, and remains competitive on the difficult 3DLoMatch benchmark.

The ablations separately examine fast filtering, three-point refinement, anchor and geometric terms, proxy construction, normal estimation, and parameter sensitivity. The runtime breakdown also helps identify where computation is spent.
The method is described with equations, an algorithm, implementation parameters, and an explicit acknowledgment of failure at extremely low inlier ratios.
weaknesses: Material: The methodological novelty is limited. The principal components are pairwise geometric-consistency filtering, a TCF-like one-point RANSAC, probability-guided three-point RANSAC borrowed from prior work, and robust ICP-style nearest-neighbor refinement. Calling their combination a new dual-space paradigm overstates the conceptual advance.

Material: The experiments do not isolate the claimed dual-space contribution against the most important simple baseline: the same filtered transformation followed by a standard robust ICP method such as FRICP. The reported 'w/o Dual-space Opt.' variant removes refinement altogether, while the anchor/geometry ablations remain inside the proposed objective. Consequently, the gains attributable to the proposed formulation rather than ordinary robust local refinement are unclear.

Material: The definitions and aggregation populations for RMSE, rotation error, and translation error are not stated. The very low errors accompanying recalls as low as 18–42% strongly suggest that errors are averaged only over successful registrations. If so, methods are evaluated on different, self-selected subsets, and lower conditional error can be obtained by failing on difficult pairs. This substantially weakens the repeated claims of state-of-the-art registration accuracy; recall is the more comparable metric, and the proposed method is not consistently best on it.

Material: The proposed one-point procedure lacks a convincing complexity or reliability analysis. Constructing Eq. (5) requires checking all pairs within an initial consensus set, potentially making each supposedly lightweight hypothesis quadratic in the number of correspondences. Moreover, the stopping probability uses the largest observed consensus as an inlier-count estimate; a structured outlier cluster can overestimate this quantity and terminate sampling prematurely. Runtime measurements on fixed benchmarks do not establish scaling or robustness of this mechanism.

Material: Several claimed innovations have only marginal ablation support. The normal constraint improves the filtered inlier ratio by roughly 0.3–0.9 percentage points, and weighted rather than random refinement changes it by only 0.02–1.47 points. The refinement stage itself provides most of the large outdoor improvement, making the evidence for the novel subcomponents comparatively weak.

Technical concern: The determinant test is described as proving that two point sets are symmetric about a plane. A negative determinant of the unconstrained orthogonal Procrustes solution only indicates that the best orthogonal fit is orientation-reversing; with noise or outliers, it does not establish planar symmetry. The resulting rejection heuristic may be useful, but its stated interpretation and validity are not justified.

Evidence/reproducibility: The method is stochastic, yet results contain no repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, random-seed protocol, or timing variability. This matters where recall differences are only a few tenths of a percentage point. Important refinement details are also deferred to another paper rather than specified fully, and Algorithm 1 contains inconsistent score indices, further hindering reproduction.

Presentation: The paper repeatedly uses unsupported superlatives such as 'perfect synergy' and infers a likely speed advantage over TurboReg without a direct CPU comparison. These claims should be replaced by precise statements restricted to measured results. Overall, the strong benchmark numbers are worthwhile, but insufficient isolation of the contribution, ambiguous accuracy evaluation, and incremental technical content make the current case favor rejection.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and practically useful coarse-to-fine registration pipeline: inexpensive geometric-consistency filtering improves the initial feature matches, while anchor-restricted geometric proxies make the subsequent ICP-like refinement less vulnerable to non-overlapping regions.

The empirical accuracy-efficiency trade-off is strong across three established benchmarks and two feature types. Examples include 84.41% recall in 0.14 s on 3DMatch with FPFH, 60.86% recall in 0.16 s on 3DLoMatch with FCGF, and 98.20% recall in 0.12 s on KITTI with FPFH. The method is often substantially faster than comparably accurate CPU baselines.

The evaluation includes component ablations, a runtime breakdown, performance by initial inlier ratio, alternative normal-estimation settings, and parameter-sensitivity experiments. Table 2 in particular supports the value of both filtering and dual-space refinement rather than attributing performance to only one stage.

The approach is training-free and implemented on CPU, making the contribution potentially useful in robotics and other latency-sensitive applications. Most implementation parameters and benchmark protocols are documented in the supplement.
The manuscript is generally clear, and it appropriately acknowledges that the method can fail when a structured outlier cluster is larger than the true inlier set.
weaknesses: There are consequential mathematical and algorithmic inconsistencies. Equations 10 and 14 minimize unsquared Euclidean norms but are claimed to admit closed-form SVD solutions; that claim holds for squared weighted residuals, not the objectives as written. Equation 15 reuses λ, already the dual-space balance weight, as a RANSAC confidence parameter; the stated KITTI value λ=1 would make log(1−λ) undefined. Algorithm 1 also updates s^(k+1) from s^(k−1), and Equation 5 does not specify the domain of the universally quantified c_k. These may be notation errors, but collectively they materially impede verification and faithful reproduction.

The novelty is moderate. Global feature matching followed by robust filtering and local geometric refinement is a familiar registration pattern; probability-weighted three-point sampling and Gaussian robust weighting are inherited from prior work. The main advance is therefore the particular one-point consensus construction and anchor-based proxy integration rather than a fundamentally new registration formulation.

RMSE, rotation error, and translation error appear to be computed only over successful registrations, but this conditioning is not explicitly stated. Because different methods succeed on different subsets, lower conditional errors do not by themselves establish uniformly more accurate registration. Reporting errors over a common subset or error distributions would better support the repeated state-of-the-art accuracy claim.

The filtering study reports only the inlier ratio of retained correspondences. It omits correspondence recall, retained-set size, and downstream registration results for several filtering variants, so the evidence does not fully show whether higher purity is achieved without discarding useful inliers. The symmetry rejection rule may also reject noisy or nearly degenerate valid configurations, but this failure mode is not analyzed.

The method is stochastic, yet results are presented without repeated-run variation or confidence intervals. This makes small differences—such as 60.86% versus 61.09% recall on 3DLoMatch with FCGF—difficult to interpret.

Parameter robustness is studied only on 3DMatch with FCGF even though α changes from 0.2 to as high as 0.95 across datasets and λ changes from 0.05 indoors to 1.0 on KITTI. Thus, the sensitivity analysis does not establish robustness of the dataset-specific choices. Runtime scope is also insufficiently explicit, and the claimed likely speed advantage over GPU-only TurboReg is extrapolated from ratios rather than directly measured.
